top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Grossman, with the citation confined to the political economy of trade protection) is my first choice. The protection-for-sale framework turned lobbying and tariff formation into a tractable equilibrium object. About three decades of theory, structural and reduced-form testing, and work on trade agreements followed from it. I apply the same test I used for Obstfeld and Rogoff: a durable framework should be judged separately from the empirical fate of one specification. By that test, the mixed record on protection-for-sale predictions limits the claim but does not disqualify it. A two-name award from a long joint programme needs no arbitrary exclusion, and the maturity of the work is not in doubt. The citation should claim the framework and the research programme it created, not confirmed predictions, and should leave out the growth strand, which may overlap with the 2025 prize (as reported in the files and not verified by me). I rank P003 second because its firm-level empirical confrontation is dense, but the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum attribution gap and its reliance on one 2003 paper keep it below P001. I rank P002 third: Autor, Dorn and Hanson is now a stable set and the work is strong, but the long-run persistence and shift-share identification are still being revised. P000 is last because P001, P002 and P003 are all substantive, mature contributions. This assessment relies on general knowledge and colleagues' written statements, not independent verification.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for Helpman and Grossman (P001), Helpman and Melitz (P003), or Autor, Dorn and Hanson (P002). Disclosed without adjudication: I am a long-running co-author of Aghion and Klenow (neither is credited on any slate proposal), and my Aghion collaboration bears on how I judge overlap with the 2025 prize. I am also an IIES colleague and frequent co-author of Krusell (secretary) and Hassler (chair), who support P001. I have not counted their preference as merit.
